The pack does not show that the bill amends or repeals RA 8435.

existing_law_overlaps.overlap: The Anti-Agricultural Sabotage Act already created a President-chaired inter-agency Anti-Agricultural Economic Sabotage Council (with an Advisory Board) dealing with smuggling, hoarding, profiteering and cartels in agricultural and fishery products; a sector-wide review commission may cover the same ground. The bill cites RA 12022 once, but the citing section is not in the pack, and nothing shown amends or abolishes the Council.

The bill names the body inconsistently: the title and s1 say 'Congressional Commission on Agriculture and Fisheries', while s4 says 'Congressional Agriculture and Fisheries Commission'.

Texts of SB-18-2485, RA-11899 and EO-127-1999 are not in the corpus (titles only); which provisions of the target follow the education-commission model, and whether SB-18-2485 became RA-11899, cannot be confirmed from the pack.

problem_diagnosis.problem: The target bill says the agriculture and fisheries sector does not lack laws, policies, programs or advisory bodies; the problem is that these are implemented in silos. It adds that advisory bodies report only to their mother departments and that their documents are not available to the public. It proposes a temporary congressional commission to review all existing programs across agencies and recommend a more integrated approach.

evidence.point: The cause of the sector's problems is fragmented, siloed implementation of existing frameworks, policies, programs and bodies.
evidence.quote: it is the fact that the frameworks, policies, programs, projects and bodies created by legislation and other national policies are currently being implemented and operationalized in silos

evidence.point: The problem is not a lack of legislation, programs or advisory bodies.
evidence.quote: it is not the absence of legislation, nor the absence of policies, programs and projects, nor the absence of advisory and consultative bodies

evidence.point: Advisory and consultative bodies answer only to their parent departments.
evidence.quote: Advisory and consultative bodies currently convened fall under the jurisdictions and report solely to their mother departments

evidence.point: Information from these bodies is not disclosed to the public.
evidence.quote: with documents and other pertinent information undisclosed and unavailable to the public even upon request

evidence.point: Congress already has two oversight committees on agriculture and fisheries created by law. The note cites the laws by number but gives no data on how those committees have performed.
evidence.quote: two congressional oversight committees on national agriculture and fisheries policy and programs have been created by law

differences.description: The stated end goal of the commission differs. The target aims its reforms at ensuring food security. The reference aims them at making the country globally competitive in agriculture and fisheries, even though the reference, not the target, puts 'Food Security' in the commission's name.
differences.target_quote: for the purpose of recommending transformative, concrete and targeted reforms in the sector with the end of ensuring food security in the Philippines
differences.reference_quote: for the purpose of recommending transformative, concrete, and targeted reforms in order to make the Philippines globally competitive in the agriculture and fisheries sector

differences.description: The target has 12 members (six per chamber); the reference has 10 (five per chamber). Members are unpaid in both bills, but travel, communications and other expenses are allowed, so the larger body in the target likely costs somewhat more.
differences.target_quote: The Commission shall be composed of twelve (12) members, with six (6) members from the Senate and six (6) members from the House of Representatives
differences.reference_quote: The AGRICOM shall be composed of ten (10) members, with five (5) members each from the Senate and the House of Representatives.

differences.description: The target makes seven committee chairpersons ex officio members: three from the Senate (agriculture, economic affairs, environment and climate change) and four from the House (agriculture, aquaculture and fisheries, agrarian reform, climate change). It names no chairperson of the commission. The reference makes the two agriculture committee chairs Co-Chairpersons, and the presiding officers designate the remaining members.

differences.reference_quote: the Chairperson of the House Committee on Agriculture and Food shall be the Co-Chairpersons of the AGRICOM.

differences.reference_quote: The AGRICOM shall appoint a recognized expert in agriculture and fisheries as Executive Director.

differences.description: Only the target names the Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS) as the commission's research arm, producing data-based research for as long as the commission exists. The bill does not say whether PIDS or the commission's appropriation pays for this work.

differences.description: The reference's objectives include operational tasks beyond review: developing and implementing training programs for farmers, and identifying markets and helping agri-businesses meet global standards. The target's objectives stay focused on reviewing and re-prioritizing programs. Compared with the reference, the target therefore likely costs less.

Because no amount is set, the cost of the target's start-up phase cannot be compared with the reference's.

baseline_corrections.note: The baseline paired the target's Effectivity clause with the reference's Repealing Clause. The OCR merged the reference's SEC. 16 Effectivity into the s15 text. Both Effectivity clauses take effect 15 days after publication, so they differ only in wording. The rule-based n_sections count (16 vs 15) comes from this OCR merge: the reference also has 16 sections.
Marked 'changed', but the Duration clauses match apart from OCR line numbers in the reference (three years from organization in both).
Marked 'changed', but the Advisory Council provisions match in substance: same eleven sector seats and same appointing authorities. The differences are wording only ('always present', 'members').

Marked 'changed', but the Technical Secretariat provisions match in substance. The cross-reference to Section 11 vs Section 5 reflects different numbering of the powers section, and the phrase on a 'competent and efficient secretariat' is wording only.
The Separability clauses differ only in wording.
The Repealing clauses differ only in the list of issuances named. The effect (repeal of inconsistent provisions) is the same. Neither bill abolishes or transfers an existing office.
The Short Titles differ only in the name ('and Food Security' in the reference). The substantive point is the purpose clause in s4/s3, recorded under differences.

In the visible text, the powers largely match: recommendations on sectoral plans, infrastructure, trainings, financing and coordination; workplan and budget approval; hearings; subpoenas. The reference lists bureaucracy review and the harmonization of DA/DAR/DENR programs as powers, while the target puts bureaucracy restructuring among its objectives (HB-20-2322:s3). Both sections are truncated.

The Declarations of Policy are framed differently: the target uses broad social-order and rural development language, the reference focuses on farmers' rights and support services. Neither changes the commission's structure, powers or funding, so this is not counted as a substantial difference.

The rule-based fact diff is correct that the head salary grade does not differ (SG 29 in both) and that membership does differ (12 vs 10). The peso_amounts difference is real: only the reference specifies P200,000,000.

output.summary: HB 2322 (20th Congress) creates the Congressional Commission on Agriculture and Fisheries (AGRICOM) (s1). Section 4 names the body differently, as a 'Congressional Agriculture and Fisheries Commission'. Mandate (s4): a comprehensive national assessment and evaluation of the performance of the agriculture and fisheries sector, to recommend transformative, concrete and targeted reforms 'with the end of ensuring food security in the Philippines'. Objectives (s3, text truncated) include re-examining public sector goals, modifying policies and public expenditures, re-prioritizing support programs, and restructuring and streamlining agriculture and fisheries-related bureaucracies. Structure: twelve members, six from the Senate and six from the House, one from each chamber representing the Minority (s5). Seven committee chairpersons are ex officio members (three Senate, four House), and the Senate President and the Speaker designate the rest (s5). Members receive no compensation, but travelling, communications and other necessary expenses are allowed (s5). The visible text names no chairperson of the Commission. Head: an Executive Director appointed by the Commission, working full-time with the rank of Executive Director IV (Salary Grade 29) (s6). The Executive Director heads a Technical Secretariat and may hire temporary, contractual or consultancy staff and set their compensation subject to civil service rules (s7). The Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS) is the research arm (s8). An Agriculture and Fisheries Legislation and Policy Advisory Council of sectoral experts is created (s9). Powers (s11, text truncated) include policy and program recommendations, approval of the workplan and budget, hearings, subpoena powers and requests for information from government offices. The Commission must accomplish its mandate within three years from its organization (s10). Funding (s13): the 'amount necessary' for initial implementation is charged against available appropriations of the Senate and the House; afterwards, continuing costs, 'including any deficiency in the current year', go in the annual General Appropriations Act. The bill states no peso amount. A general repealing clause is included (s15). The visible text does not abolish or transfer any existing office.
output.history: Taken only from the research agent output. Same-Congress related measures: SB-20-1199, the Senate counterpart, matches the target almost word for word (12 members, same committee chairs, Executive Director at SG 29, same powers and appropriations sections). HB-20-5296 and HB-20-5129 are near-copies refiled in the House; both add 'Food Security' to the name. HB-20-11060 is a competing House design that keeps 12 members but adds co-chairpersons, an expanded mandate and a Technical Secretariat, and calls the body independent and temporary. SB-20-1345 is a competing Senate design: agriculture only, 10 members, co-chairpersons, and a fixed appropriation. A Senate committee report (CR-20-AGRICOM) recommends SB-20-1624 in substitution of SB 1199 and SB 1345. SB-20-1624 is now the Senate vehicle. It shrinks the body to 10 members with co-chairpersons and sets a fixed initial appropriation. The committee report front matter shown does not mention HB 2322. Possible precedents, matched on title only (texts not reviewed): RA-11899 (Congressional Commission on Education; the target's title follows its title almost exactly) and SB-18-2485 (18th Congress, status 'Lapsed Into Law'). EO-127-1999 was judged unrelated. Status: the pack does not give authors, filing dates, committee referrals or the current status of HB 2322 or of the other 20th Congress bills. It contains no House committee report or substitute bill, so whether HB 2322 has been consolidated cannot be established, and no earlier-Congress AGRICOM bill was found.
output.differences: Taken only from the diagnosis agent output, which compared the target with SB-20-1624 (the Senate substitute). Verdict: 'partly different'. Substantial differences: (1) Mandate goal: the target aims its reforms at ensuring food security (s4). The reference aims at making the Philippines globally competitive in agriculture and fisheries (SB-20-1624:s3). (2) Size: 12 members in the target (s5), 10 in the reference (SB-20-1624:s7). Members are unpaid in both, but expenses are allowed, so the larger body likely costs somewhat more. (3) Leadership: the target makes seven committee chairs ex officio members and names no chairperson. The reference makes the two agriculture committee chairs Co-Chairpersons. (4) Executive Director: SG 29 and full-time in both; the target adds qualifications (citizenship, probity, independence, relevant experience) (s6). (5) Research arm: only the target names PIDS (s8), and it does not say who pays for that work (fiscal direction unclear). (6) Assessment scope: only the reference lists what the national assessment must cover (agency compliance with mandates, hindering factors, best practices, M&E plan, LGU role). The target's scope is more general. (7) Operational tasks: the reference's objectives include developing and implementing farmer training programs and market support. The target stays focused on review and re-prioritization, so it likely costs less than the reference on this point. (8) Standing committees: in the target they may be chaired by members or by multisectoral experts (s12); in the reference each must be chaired by a member. (9) Initial funding: the reference fixes an initial amount charged to Senate and House appropriations. The target charges an unspecified 'amount necessary' to the same source (s13), so the two start-up costs cannot be compared. (10) Deficiency clause: only the target lets the GAA cover 'any deficiency in the current year' (s13), which the diagnosis agent rates as likely to raise cost. The diagnosis agent judged several sections that a baseline marked 'changed' to match in substance or differ only in wording: Technical Secretariat, Advisory Council, Duration (three years in both), Separability, Repealing and Effectivity.
output.existing_law: From the research agent and the bill's own references. (1) RA 8435 (Agriculture and Fisheries Modernization Act): s13 already requires a medium- and long-term Agriculture and Fisheries Modernization Plan, and s14 covers food security plans. AGRICOM's recommendations on sectoral plans and targets (HB-20-2322:s11) would overlap with this planning mandate, although AGRICOM's role is recommendatory. (2) RA 12022 (Anti-Agricultural Sabotage Act): s15 created a President-chaired Anti-Agricultural Economic Sabotage Council, which deals with smuggling, hoarding, profiteering and cartels. A sector-wide review commission may cover the same ground. The bill cites RA 8435 and RA 12022 once each, but neither citation appears in the visible section text (s3 and s11 are truncated). Nothing visible amends, repeals or abolishes either law or the Council; the only repeal provision is the general clause in s15. (3) According to the diagnosis agent, the bill's explanatory note says two congressional oversight committees on agriculture and fisheries policy and programs have already been created by law. (4) The bill names PIDS as research arm and lets it coordinate with existing advisory and consultative bodies under the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Science and Technology (s8). These are existing bodies whose work could overlap with AGRICOM's. (5) Note on inputs: the research agent reported that only some sections were in its pack. The target section text supplied here runs from s1 to s16, with s3 and s11 truncated.

fiscal.narrative: The costing engine gives an order-of-magnitude range for the first full year, treating the body as a 'commission'. The range runs from PHP 28879960 to PHP 545174905. The engine says this is 'not a costing for budget purposes'. It uses two methods. Method A (bottom-up) builds the cost from salaries and benefits: a head at SG-29, an assumed headcount of 30 to 130, assumed average staff salary grades SG-13 to SG-18 at Step 1, statutory benefits and allowances, and MOOE at 35%-60% of personnel cost. Method A gives PHP 28879960 to PHP 190266767, of which personnel is PHP 21392563 to PHP 118916730. Method B (comparators) applies per-staff costs from 2025 COA audit reports of the National Water Resources Board (2454812.646181818 per staff) and the Climate Change Commission (4193653.116612903 per staff). Method B gives PHP 73644379 to PHP 545174905. The bill itself states no peso amount (the engine's 'stated_in_bill' is empty). Section 13 charges only 'the amount necessary' for initial implementation to available Senate and House appropriations, with later and deficiency amounts to come through the annual GAA. There is therefore no bill figure to compare the engine range with. Fit cautions for the reviewer: (a) The entity type comes from the title. AGRICOM is a temporary congressional commission: it has three years to accomplish its mandate (s10), its members are unpaid (s5), and its secretariat staff may be temporary, contractual or on consultancy (s7). Both comparators are executive-branch bodies with authorized plantilla positions, so the headcount of 30-130 is taken from the comparators, not from the bill. (b) The listed assumptions do not cover members' allowable travel, communications and other expenses (s5), any costs of the Advisory Council (s9) or the PIDS research-arm work (s8), hearings, or consultations. (c) The engine covers the first full year only. It gives no total for the three-year duration, and none is computed here. (d) The engine excludes capital outlay. Several benefit assumptions are marked 'to verify', and the staff salary grade and MOOE share are marked for reviewer confirmation.

risks: Staffing and absorptive capacity: both comparators had unfilled authorized positions in 2025. NWRB had 124 authorized and 110 filled; the Climate Change Commission had 76 authorized and 62 filled (source: COA Annual Audit Reports 2025 Executive Summaries, comparator table; figures 'reviewer to confirm'). With only three years to accomplish its mandate (HB-20-2322:s10) and staff who may be temporary, contractual or on consultancy (s7), AGRICOM may face similar or greater difficulty filling posts quickly.

Budget utilization: in 2025, obligations were below allotments at both comparators. NWRB had allotments of 310445046.28 and obligations of 270029391.08; CCC had allotments of 271494591 and obligations of 260006493.23 (source: COA Annual Audit Reports 2025 Executive Summaries, comparator table; reviewer to confirm). A newly organized temporary body may also under-spend in its first year.

Open-ended funding: s13 sets no initial amount, and it allows the GAA to cover 'any deficiency in the current year'. The diagnosis agent notes this leaves the start-up cost unstated and harder to control (source: HB-20-2322:s13; Agent 2 design options and differences).
Unfunded workload: s8 assigns PIDS to be the research arm with no stated funding arrangement, which shifts work to PIDS (source: HB-20-2322:s8; Agent 2 gaps and design options).

Possible duplication with existing mandates: the RA 8435 planning mandate (RA-8435:s13), the Anti-Agricultural Economic Sabotage Council under RA 12022 (RA-12022:s15), the two existing congressional oversight committees on agriculture and fisheries mentioned in the explanatory note, and DA/DOST advisory bodies (source: Agent 1 existing-law overlaps; Agent 2 problem diagnosis; HB-20-2322:s8).

Governance: the visible text names no chairperson of the Commission. Nine of its twelve seats go to ex officio committee chairs or designated members drawn from both chambers. The diagnosis agent flags the lack of a designated leader as a trade-off (source: HB-20-2322:s5; Agent 2 design options and gaps).

Legal drafting inconsistency: the body's name differs between s1 ('Congressional Commission on Agriculture and Fisheries') and s4 ('Congressional Agriculture and Fisheries Commission'), which may create ambiguity in implementation (source: HB-20-2322:s1, s4; Agent 1 gaps).

output.label: AI-assisted preliminary draft for DBM reviewer validation. Not an official position.

issues.problem: The draft says HB-20-11060 'adds co-chairpersons, an expanded mandate and a Technical Secretariat' compared with the target. The target already creates a Technical Secretariat headed by the Executive Director, so a Technical Secretariat is not a difference. The draft's own differences section also counts the Technical Secretariat as matching in substance. The co-chairpersons and expanded-mandate parts have no citation either. The only cited HB-20-11060 text is s4 ('independent, temporary...').
issues.evidence: HB-20-2322:s7 'A Technical Secretariat, to be headed by the Executive Director, shall be organized to provide technical and administrative support to the Commission'; only HB-20-11060:s4 is cited

issues.type: overstated certainty / status not in inputs
issues.where: history ('SB-20-1624 is now the Senate vehicle')
issues.problem: The draft states as fact that SB-20-1624 is the current Senate vehicle. The only support is that a committee report recommends it in substitution. The draft itself says the pack gives no current status for 20th Congress bills, and the checklist asks the reviewer to 'Confirm the status of SB 1624 and the Senate committee report'. The sentence should say that the report recommends it, not that it is the vehicle.
issues.evidence: CR-20-AGRICOM:note 'Recommending its approval in substitution of Senate Bill Nos. 1199 and 1345'; status of SB-20-1624: not in inputs

issues.problem: The draft contrasts the target (food security) with the reference (global competitiveness), which implies the target leaves out competitiveness. But the target's own objectives explicitly include raising global competitiveness. The difference is one of emphasis in s4, not a different goal, and the verdict 'partly different' relies partly on this item.
issues.evidence: HB-20-2322:s3(b) 'with the ultimate goal of raising the productivity and the global competitiveness of our local agriculture and fisheries subsectors'

issues.where: differences items (3), (4), (6), (8), (9), (10) and the 'Duration (three years in both)' statement; history details for SB-20-1199, HB-20-5296/5129, SB-20-1345, SB-20-1624
issues.problem: Most statements about the reference and related bills have no supporting citation in the claims list. These include: SB-20-1624 Co-Chairpersons, ED at SG 29 and full-time, assessment-scope list, member-chaired standing committees, fixed initial appropriation, absence of a deficiency clause, and three-year duration. They also include SB-20-1199 having the 'same committee chairs, Executive Director at SG 29, same powers and appropriations sections', HB-20-5296/5129 adding 'Food Security' to the name, SB-20-1345 being 'agriculture only' with co-chairpersons and a fixed appropriation, and SB-18-2485's 'Lapsed Into Law' status. The only cited reference/related sections are SB-20-1624:s3, s4, s7; SB-20-1199:s4; HB-20-5296:s5; HB-20-5129:s13; SB-20-1345:s5. The draft also never gives the reference's fixed peso amount, so the 'fixed initial amount' claims cannot be checked.
issues.evidence: claims list contains no section for these statements; texts of SB-20-1624 (other than s3, s4, s7), SB-20-1199 (other than s4), SB-18-2485: not in inputs

issues.where: fiscal.assumptions (headcount and entity type) and fiscal.narrative caution (a)
issues.problem: The draft's assumptions table marks 'Headcount 30-130' and 'Entity type: commission' as to_verify: false, yet the bill sets no staffing pattern and the narrative itself questions whether the entity type fits. The narrative also says the 30-130 headcount 'is taken from the comparators'. That is only partly true: the comparators have 76 (CCC) and 124 (NWRB) authorized positions, so the low end of 30 has no stated source. The engine does not attach a to_verify flag to these items, so the draft's 'false' values are its own judgment, and they understate uncertainty in the inputs that drive the whole range.
issues.evidence: engine assumptions: 'Headcount 30-130' source 'Climate Change Commission has 76 authorized positions (COA 2025); NWRB 124'; HB-20-2322:s7 sets no number of staff

issues.type: fiscal narrative omits key fit caution
issues.problem: The draft does not explain what Method B's per-staff cost contains. The figures in the draft's own risks section show that per-staff = total 2025 obligations / filled positions: NWRB 270,029,391.08/110 = 2,454,812.65 and CCC 260,006,493.23/62 = 4,193,653.12. Method B therefore loads all program and operating spending of two executive agencies, possibly including capital outlay, onto each AGRICOM staff member. Yet the engine says it excludes capital outlay. It also divides by filled positions but applies the result to a headcount based on authorized positions. Method B sets the top of the range (PHP 545,174,905), so the reviewer should be told that the upper bound is probably the least representative figure for a recommendatory congressional body.
issues.evidence: engine method_b_comparators per_staff 2454812.646181818 and 4193653.116612903; draft risks: NWRB obligations 270029391.08, filled 110; CCC obligations 260006493.23, filled 62; engine caveat 'Excludes capital outlay'

issues.problem: The filled-position counts (110, 62) and allotment/obligation amounts (310,445,046.28; 270,029,391.08; 271,494,591; 260,006,493.23) do not appear in the costing engine output or the bill. The comparator table they are attributed to was not supplied for this check. They agree with the engine's per-staff figures (see above), and the draft marks them 'reviewer to confirm', but they could not be checked here against their source.
issues.evidence: not in inputs (comparator table not supplied); engine gives only authorized positions 76 and 124 and per_staff values

issues.problem: The narrative does not repeat the engine's caveat that the range excludes transfers of existing personnel and budgets from abolished offices. It also does not state the consequence for this bill: nothing is abolished or transferred, so no offset reduces the net new cost and the gross range is also the net new cost. The engine's exclusion of 'regional offices beyond the comparators' scale' is also left out. Quoting the range to the last peso (PHP 28879960 to PHP 545174905) implies more precision than an 'order-of-magnitude' estimate supports.
issues.evidence: engine caveats: 'Excludes capital outlay, regional offices beyond the comparators' scale, and transfers of existing personnel and budgets from abolished offices (which reduce the net new cost)'; draft summary 'The visible text does not abolish or transfer any existing office'

issues.type: engine assumptions may not fit staff type
issues.problem: Caution (a) flags the comparator headcount, but not that Method A's benefit stack assumes regular plantilla employees paid on the salary schedule. The benefits are year-end and mid-year bonuses, GSIS 12%, PhilHealth, PERA, Pag-IBIG, ECC, clothing allowance, cash gift and PEI. Section 7 instead lets the ED hire temporary, contractual or consultancy personnel and 'determine their compensation', and s11(b) has the Commission approve 'compensation of all personnel'. For this body the cost structure could therefore differ from Method A's in either direction.
issues.evidence: HB-20-2322:s7 'whether temporary, contractual, or on consultancy, and determine their compensation'; HB-20-2322:s11(b) 'including compensation of all personnel'; engine benefit assumptions

issues.where: risks (Governance item: 'Nine of its twelve seats go to ex officio committee chairs or designated members drawn from both chambers'); summary and claim ('the Senate President and the Speaker designate the rest')
issues.problem: The 'nine of twelve' count is not stated in the bill. It holds only if it means 7 committee chairs plus 2 Minority designees and assumes no chair is a Minority member. As written, all twelve seats are chairs or designated legislators, so the sentence is unclear. Also, not every non-ex officio member is designated by the Senate President or Speaker, because the Minority member from each chamber is designated by the Minority Leader. The draft misses that only about 2 Senate and 1 House seats are left to the presiding officers, and that the bill does not say how the count works if a committee chair belongs to the Minority.
issues.evidence: HB-20-2322:s5 'one of the six (6) members coming from each House shall represent the Minority as designated by the Minority Leader of each House'; 3 Senate and 4 House chairs listed in s5

issues.problem: The draft names only PIDS as carrying unfunded work. It misses that s11(e) lets the Commission require any government department, bureau or office to prepare reports and submit recommendations or plans. It also misses that s9 puts two officials from government agriculture and fisheries agencies and two LGU heads on an 11-member Advisory Council whose members 'shall always be present in all meetings'. Both shift workload and costs to executive agencies and LGUs, which the draft does not mention.
issues.evidence: HB-20-2322:s11(e) 'Secure from any department, bureau, office or instrumentality of the government technical information, preparation and production of reports, and the submission of recommendations or plans'; HB-20-2322:s9 composition (3+2+2+2+2) and 'shall always be present in all meetings'

issues.problem: The open-ended funding risk does not mention that the Commission approves its own budget and all disbursements, including compensation of all personnel (s11(b)). Together with the unstated initial amount and the deficiency clause in s13, this weakens external control over spending. Section 7 (the ED determines compensation) and s11(b) (the Commission approves compensation) also divide that authority without saying how they fit together.
issues.evidence: HB-20-2322:s11(b) 'the budget for the programs of the Commission and all disbursements therefrom, including compensation of all personnel'; HB-20-2322:s13; HB-20-2322:s7

issues.type: incomplete note on truncation / possible missed provision
issues.problem: The draft says only s3 and s11 are truncated. Section 9 also ends mid-provision with no closing punctuation ('...engaged in agriculture and fisheries'), so any text on Advisory Council compensation or expenses may be missing. The draft's statements that the bill cites RA 8435 and RA 12022 'once each' cannot be checked against the supplied sections. The same applies to the RA 8435 s14 food-security plans and the RA 12022 Council's smuggling, hoarding and cartel functions, which have no citation.
issues.evidence: HB-20-2322:s9 text ends 'civil society organizations and development partners engaged in agriculture and fisheries'; RA-8435:s14 and RA-12022 Council functions: not in inputs; only RA-8435:s13 and RA-12022:s15 (creation/chair) are cited

issues.where: fiscal.narrative caution (a) ('AGRICOM is a temporary congressional commission') and existing_law item (1) ('AGRICOM's role is recommendatory')
issues.problem: The bill never calls the body 'temporary' and has no explicit dissolution clause. Section 10 only requires the Commission to accomplish its mandate within three years; 'temporary' is HB-20-11060's wording. Its objectives are also worded as direct action, not recommendation: 'Modify agriculture and fisheries policies and public expenditures', 'Restructure and streamline ... bureaucracies'. The draft should note that the duration and recommendatory nature are inferred from the bill, not stated in it, and that extensions are therefore possible.
issues.evidence: HB-20-2322:s10 'The Commission shall accomplish its mandate within three (3) years from its organization'; HB-20-2322:s3(b), s3(d); HB-20-11060:s4 'independent, temporary'
